title: Lesson 0: how a processor runs a loop
description:
A short guided tour of RVCAT with one example, the loop VectSum:
from the C code to machine instructions, latency, overlapped execution, dependences and performance bounds.

About 20 minutes; optional cards go deeper.

tutorial.name: Lesson 0: how a processor runs a loop

steps.title: Welcome to RVCAT
steps.description:
RVCAT explains why a loop takes the time it takes.

This lesson follows one example and shows the simulator little by little.

• Continue follows the main path; In depth cards explain more, for those who need it.

• The bar above counts the questions and predictions.

• Exit lesson leaves it at any time; it is always in the 📘 Lessons menu.

steps.title: 1. The loop VectSum
steps.description:
Click the table header to see the C code (needed to continue):
the function adds all the N elements of two vectors, V and W.

Time grows with N: T = T0 + T1·N (T0: constant time outside the loop; T1: time per iteration).
VectSum has linear time complexity, Θ(N): doubling N approximately doubles the time.
Complexity does not depend on the processor; the constant T1 does.

Measured on a real processor (Intel Core i5-12400), each loop iteration takes 4 clock cycles.
Where do those 4 cycles come from?
      That is the question of this lesson.

validation.message: Click the header of the table to see the C code

steps.title: In depth: time, cycles and complexity
steps.description:
• The processor works at the rate of a clock: one cycle typically lasts 0.2 to 1 ns (1 to 5 GHz).
   We measure time in cycles: seconds = cycles / frequency.

• Real measurements (Intel Core i5-12400, N = 5000):
        20,020 cycles = 4 cycles per iteration (4.57 microseconds at 4.38 GHz).

steps.title: 2. From C to machine instructions
steps.description:
The compiler translates the C loop into machine instructions,
the simple operations that a given processor (its ISA) executes.
RVCAT shows machine instructions in a readable form, one per row:
• two loads (read V[i] and W[i] from memory),
• two additions of floats (sum = sum + tmp),
• and the loop control (i = i + 1, compare, branch):
      7 instructions per iteration.

steps.title: In depth: what the compiler can do
steps.description:
The compiler can transform the code to run faster, and the programmer controls it in two ways:

• (A) enabling or disabling strategies with options (flags) added to the compilation command of gcc
   or another compiler, e.g. gcc -O2 vectsum.c, or -ffast-math, which allows changing
   the order of floating-point additions (it can change the rounding);

• (B) rewriting the source code by hand to make the compiler's task easier.

The versions V1 and V2 that you will see are examples of (B).
nextLabels: In depth: machine instructions and ISA

steps.title: In depth: machine instructions and ISA
steps.description:
A machine instruction is a simple operation, coded in binary, that the processor executes directly:
read or write a memory location, an arithmetic operation, a comparison, a branch to another instruction.

An Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the specification of the machine instructions that a family of processors
executes: their operations, operands, registers, memory addressing and binary format.
A program compiled for an ISA runs on every processor that implements it, whatever its internal design.

Common ISAs: x86-64 (Intel and AMD: PCs and servers), ARM (AArch64: phones, Apple computers, servers)
and RISC-V (an open and free ISA: embedded systems, research, a growing number of processors).

RVCAT does not model a real ISA: it simulates abstract instructions, similar in all of them.
The next optional cards show the machine code (assembly) of the loop of Base in each ISA.

steps.title: In depth: the loop of Base in x86-64
steps.description:
Machine code (assembly) of the loop, compiled with gcc -O2 (simplified; it may change with the compiler version):

.L3:                                    // RVCAT rows
  addss  xmm0, DWORD PTR [rdi+rax*4]    // 0, 1: tmp = V[i]; sum = sum + tmp
  addss  xmm0, DWORD PTR [rsi+rax*4]    // 2, 3: tmp = W[i]; sum = sum + tmp
  add    rax, 1                         // 4: i = i + 1
  cmp    rdx, rax                       // 5: c = i != N
  jne    .L3                            // 6: if c go back

x86-64 can combine a load and an addition in one instruction (an operand in memory): 5 instructions.
Inside, the processor splits them into simple operations (micro-operations), like the 7 rows of RVCAT.

steps.title: In depth: the loop of Base in ARM (AArch64)
steps.description:
Machine code (assembly) of the loop, compiled with gcc -O2 (simplified; it may change with the compiler version):

.L3:                                    // RVCAT rows
  ldr    s1, [x0, x3, lsl 2]            // 0: tmp = V[i]
  ldr    s2, [x1, x3, lsl 2]            // 2: tmp = W[i]
  add    x3, x3, 1                      // 4: i = i + 1
  fadd   s0, s0, s1                     // 1: sum = sum + tmp
  cmp    x2, x3                         // 5: c = i != N
  fadd   s0, s0, s2                     // 3: sum = sum + tmp
  bne    .L3                            // 6: if c go back

ARM loads and computes in separate instructions: 7 instructions, one for each row of RVCAT.

steps.title: In depth: the loop of Base in RISC-V
steps.description:
Machine code (assembly) of the loop, compiled with gcc -O2 (simplified; it may change with the compiler version):

.L3:                                    # RVCAT rows
  flw     fa4, 0(a0)                    # 0: tmp = V[i]
  flw     fa5, 0(a1)                    # 2: tmp = W[i]
  addi    a0, a0, 4                     # 4: next element of V
  addi    a1, a1, 4                     #    next element of W
  fadd.s  fa0, fa0, fa4                 # 1: sum = sum + tmp
  fadd.s  fa0, fa0, fa5                 # 3: sum = sum + tmp
  bne     a0, a2, .L3                   # 5, 6: if not at the end, go back

Also 7 instructions, but different: the compiler advances two pointers instead of the index i,
and one branch instruction (bne) compares and jumps.

steps.title: 3. Measure: simulate the loop
steps.description:
Simulate N = 1,000 iterations of the loop on a processor similar to the real one:
click the button (or ▶ Show me).
steps.doneDescription:
{{instructions}} instructions in {{cycles}} cycles: {{cyclesPerIter}} cycles per iteration, like the real processor.

IPC = {{ipc}} instructions per cycle: the processor executes almost 2 instructions every cycle.

Key: current processors can execute multiple instructions at the same time (Instruction-Level Parallelism, ILP).

Want to improve performance? Next come two versions of VectSum rewritten by hand: before simulating them, predict their time.

steps.title: In depth: a processor that executes several instructions at once
steps.description:
The program is a sequence of instructions, but the processor does not have to execute them one by one.

A multiple-issue (superscalar) processor starts and finishes several instructions per cycle (this one, up to 4),
has several execution units working in parallel, and keeps many instructions in flight, each one at a different stage.

It finds by itself which instructions are independent and overlaps them; the result is the same as executing them in order.

So IPC can be greater than 1, but only if there are enough independent instructions: the rest of the lesson shows what limits it.

steps.title: Predict: version V1
steps.description:
V1 only changes the order of the additions:   sum = sum + (V[i] + W[i]).

It still has 7 instructions per iteration (look at the table).

Base takes 4 cycles per iteration.
How many cycles per iteration will V1 take?

Click the table header to see the C code of V1 (needed to continue).

Write your prediction, save it, and simulate.

validation.message: Click the header of the table to see the C code

steps.title: Predict: version V2
steps.description:
V2 is unrolled: each iteration adds two elements of each vector (i = i + 2),
with 11 instructions instead of 2 × 7 = 14: fewer instructions per element.
How many cycles per element (cycles/iter ÷ 2) will V2 take?

steps.title: A paradox?
steps.questionText: Per element: Base runs 7 instructions in 4 cycles, V1 runs 7 instructions in 2 cycles, and V2 runs 5.5 instructions in 4 cycles (the same on the real processor). Which statement is true?

answers.text: The number of instructions alone does not determine the time
answers.explanation: Right: V1 is twice as fast with the same instructions, and V2 is not faster with fewer. We need a model of how the processor executes them.
V2 executes fewer instructions per element than Base, and takes the same time.

answers.text: Changing the order of the additions cannot change the time
answers.explanation: V1 only changes that order, and runs twice as fast.

answers.text: Half the iterations means half the time
answers.explanation: V2 does half the iterations, but each one does twice the work: same time per element.

steps.title: 4. Latency
steps.description:
The processor is now shown. Each type of instruction takes a fixed number of cycles
to execute: its latency. Here: load 4, float addition 2, integer operations and branch 1.
(The type button of the Program panel shows the latency of each instruction.)
The processor executes instructions in ports P1…P4: each one starts one instruction per cycle.

steps.title: One instruction at a time
steps.questionText: Imagine a processor that handles one instruction at a time: Dispatch (1 cycle), Execute (its latency) and Write the result (1 cycle), and only then the next instruction. How many cycles does one iteration of Base take (2 loads, 2 float additions, 3 integer/branch)?
steps.numericCorrect: Right: 2 × (1+4+1) + 2 × (1+2+1) + 3 × (1+1+1) = 12 + 8 + 9 = 29 cycles. Seven times more than the 4 measured!
steps.numericWrong: Each instruction takes 1 + latency + 1 cycles, and they do not overlap: add the 7 instructions.

steps.title: Check it: the timeline
steps.description:
This processor has been reduced to one instruction in flight (ROB = 1, dispatch 1).
The Timeline shows each instruction (rows) cycle by cycle (columns):
D dispatch · E execute (L for a load) · W write the result · R retire (leaves the processor).
One iteration takes 29 cycles: {{cyclesPerIter}} cycles/iter in the simulation.

steps.title: 5. Overlap: two instructions at once
steps.description:
Now 2 instructions can be in flight (ROB = 2): while one executes, the next one is dispatched,
like a car wash with several stages. Time drops to {{cyclesPerIter}} cycles per iteration.
The dots . mean that an instruction waits for the result of a previous one.

steps.title: In depth: pipelining
steps.description:
• Pipelining divides the processing of an instruction in stages that work at the same time,
   each one on a different instruction (an assembly line).
• A bypass gives the result of an instruction directly to the next one that needs it.
• An instruction can start executing only when its input data are ready: a data dependence.
• With ROB = 2 the time is close to the sum of the latencies: 4+2+4+2+1+1+1 = 15, plus some cycles.

steps.title: A real processor: many instructions at once
steps.description:
Back to the real configuration: up to {{dispatch}} instructions dispatched per cycle,
up to {{rob}} in flight, executed out of order as soon as their data are ready (and retired in order).
Instructions of different iterations overlap (one colour per iteration):
the loop runs at {{cyclesPerIter}} cycles per iteration.

steps.title: In depth: out-of-order execution
steps.description:
• Instructions wait in a buffer until their input data are ready (.) and a port is free (*).
• The ROB (reorder buffer) keeps them in program order: they retire in order (R),
   so the result is the same as a sequential execution. - means: executed, waiting to retire.
• The ROB size limits how many instructions are in flight: the execution window.
• Dispatch / retire width and the ports limit how many instructions are processed per cycle.

steps.title: 6. The critical path
steps.description:
Critical marks in red the chain of instructions that determines the time.
Each addition to sum needs the result of the previous one, also across iterations:
sum → sum → sum… Two additions of 2 cycles per iteration: 2 + 2 = 4 cycles.
Every other instruction executes for free, overlapped with this chain.

steps.title: Why is V1 twice as fast?
steps.questionText: V1 computes tmp = V[i] + W[i] and then sum = sum + tmp. Why does it take 2 cycles per iteration instead of 4?

answers.text: Only one addition per iteration depends on the previous iteration: the chain of sum has 2 cycles
answers.explanation: Yes: V[i] + W[i] does not depend on sum, so it overlaps with the chain.
No: V1 executes the same 7 instructions per iteration.

answers.text: The additions of V1 have a lower latency
answers.explanation: No: they are the same float additions, of 2 cycles.
It uses the same ports; the difference is the chain of dependences.

steps.title: Experiment: a faster addition
steps.description:
Make Base run below 2.5 cycles per iteration changing only the latency of FLOAT.ADD.
In the Processor panel, click show operation types, then the FLOAT cell, and change its latency;
then simulate (Simulation panel). Predict first: what latency do you need?

steps.title: 7. Two bounds on performance
steps.description:
Static Analysis computes, without simulating, two lower bounds of the time per iteration:
• latency bound: the longest cyclic chain of dependences (sum: {{latencyBound}} cycles);
• throughput bound: the busiest resource (here port P2, with the 2 loads: {{throughputBound}}).
Minimum time = max(latency bound, throughput bound) = {{minTime}} cycles per iteration.

steps.title: In depth: the dependence graph
steps.description:
• The dependence graph shows one box per iteration and the arrows of the data dependences.
• Cyclic dependences, in red, cross iterations: they set the latency bound.
• Click a row of Latency bounds to highlight its chain (▶ Show me does it for sum).

steps.title: The bounds of V2
steps.questionText: Look at the static analysis of V2 (selected now). What is its minimum time per iteration, in cycles?
steps.numericCorrect: Right: the chain of sum has 4 additions of 2 cycles = {{latencyBound}} cycles per iteration of 2 elements: 4 cycles per element, like Base. Unrolling did not shorten the chain.
steps.numericWrong: Take the maximum of the latency bound and the throughput bound of V2.

steps.title: 8. Summary
steps.description:
• The compiler turns C into machine instructions; you can help it (options, rewriting the code).
• Time does not follow the number of instructions nor the sum of their latencies:
   a modern processor overlaps them, and the dependences set the pace.
• Minimum time = max(latency bound, throughput bound): find what limits your loop first.
